subject: Operating Systems
explanation: A process is a program in execution. It is an active entity that requires system resources such as CPU time, memory, files, and I/O devices to accomplish its task. Unlike a program, which is a passive entity stored on disk, a process is dynamic and has its own execution context.
key_points: A process is a program in execution (active entity)
Each process has its own Process Control Block (PCB)
A process can be in one of several states: New, Ready, Running, Waiting, Terminated
Processes require system resources: CPU, memory, I/O devices
The OS is responsible for process creation, scheduling, and termination
Processes communicate via Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
examples: A running web browser like Chrome is a process
A running Python script is a process
When you open Microsoft Word, the OS creates a process for it

subject: Operating Systems
explanation: A thread is the smallest unit of CPU execution within a process. A process can have multiple threads, all sharing the same memory space and resources of the parent process. Threads within a process run concurrently and share code, data, and OS resources.
key_points: A thread is a lightweight sub-process
Threads share the memory and resources of their parent process
Each thread has its own stack, registers, and program counter
Multi-threading improves application performance and responsiveness
Context switching between threads is faster than between processes
Types: User-level threads and Kernel-level threads
examples: A web browser uses separate threads for rendering, network requests, and user interface
A word processor uses one thread for typing input and another for spell-checking

subject: Operating Systems
explanation: CPU Scheduling is the process by which the OS decides which process gets the CPU at any given time. Since only one process can run on a CPU core at a time, scheduling is essential for efficient CPU utilization and fair resource allocation.
key_points: Goal: Maximize CPU utilization and throughput, minimize waiting and response time
FCFS (First Come First Served): Simple, non-preemptive, can cause convoy effect
SJF (Shortest Job First): Optimal average waiting time, may cause starvation
Round Robin: Each process gets equal time slices (quantum), suitable for time-sharing
Priority Scheduling: Higher priority processes run first, can cause starvation
Multilevel Queue: Processes divided into groups with separate queues
examples: Round Robin with quantum=4ms: P1 runs 4ms, then P2 runs 4ms, then P3, cycling back
In SJF, if processes have burst times 8, 4, 9, 5, the order is P2, P4, P1, P3

subject: Operating Systems
explanation: A deadlock is a situation where a set of processes are blocked because each process is holding a resource and waiting to acquire a resource held by another process. No process can make progress.
key_points: Four necessary conditions (Coffman): Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait
Deadlock Prevention: Eliminate one of the four conditions
Deadlock Avoidance: Banker Algorithm - only allocate if state remains safe
Deadlock Detection: Allow deadlock, detect it, and recover
Resource Allocation Graph (RAG) is used to detect deadlocks
Recovery: Process termination or resource preemption
examples: Process A holds Printer and waits for Scanner; Process B holds Scanner and waits for Printer - deadlock!
Two trains on the same track heading toward each other - neither can move

subject: Operating Systems
explanation: Paging is a memory management technique that eliminates external fragmentation by dividing physical memory into fixed-sized frames and logical memory into pages of the same size.
key_points: Physical memory divided into fixed-size blocks called frames
Logical memory divided into blocks of same size called pages
Page table maps logical page numbers to physical frame numbers
Eliminates external fragmentation but causes internal fragmentation
Page size is typically 4KB in modern systems
TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) caches recent page table entries for speed
examples: If page size = 4KB and a process needs 13KB, it gets 4 pages (internal fragmentation in last page)
Logical address is split into page number and offset to find physical address

subject: Operating Systems
explanation: Virtual memory is a memory management technique that gives each process the illusion of having a large contiguous address space even when physical RAM is limited. It uses disk space as an extension of RAM.
key_points: Allows execution of programs larger than physical memory
Uses disk space (swap space) as extended memory
Demand paging: pages loaded into memory only when needed
Page fault occurs when a required page is not in memory
Page replacement algorithms: FIFO, LRU, Optimal
Thrashing occurs when too much time is spent paging in/out
examples: A 4GB program can run on a system with 2GB RAM using virtual memory
When Windows slows down with many programs open, the page file (virtual memory) is being used

subject: DBMS
explanation: A database is an organized collection of structured data stored electronically. A DBMS (Database Management System) is software that provides an interface to store, retrieve, and manage data.
key_points: Database: organized collection of related data
DBMS: software to manage the database (MySQL, Oracle, SQLite, PostgreSQL)
Advantages: Data sharing, reduced redundancy, data integrity, security, backup
Types: Relational (tables), NoSQL (documents, graphs, key-value), hierarchical
Schema: structure/blueprint of the database
Instance: actual data stored at a particular moment
examples: A university database storing student records, courses, and grades
An e-commerce database storing product catalog, orders, and customer information
MySQL, Oracle, SQLite are popular DBMS software

subject: DBMS
explanation: A primary key is a column or combination of columns in a table that uniquely identifies each row. It cannot contain NULL values and must be unique for every record.
key_points: Uniquely identifies each record in a table
Cannot have NULL values
Cannot have duplicate values
A table can have only one primary key
Can be a single column or composite (multiple columns)
Often implemented as auto-increment integers
examples: Student_ID in a Students table (each student has a unique ID)
Employee_ID in an Employees table
Email address can be a primary key if each user has a unique email

subject: DBMS
explanation: A foreign key is a column in one table that references the primary key of another table. It establishes a relationship between two tables and enforces referential integrity.
key_points: Creates a link between two tables
References the primary key of another (parent) table
Enforces referential integrity
Can have NULL values (unless specified NOT NULL)
The child table cannot have a value not present in the parent table
Prevents orphaned records
examples: Orders table has Customer_ID as foreign key referencing Customers table
Enrollment table has Student_ID (FK to Students) and Course_ID (FK to Courses)
You cannot add an order for a customer that does not exist

subject: DBMS
explanation: Normalization is the process of organizing a relational database to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity. It involves dividing large tables into smaller ones according to Normal Forms: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF.
key_points: 1NF: Each column must contain atomic values; no repeating groups
2NF: Must be in 1NF + every non-key attribute fully depends on entire primary key
3NF: Must be in 2NF + no transitive dependencies
BCNF: Stronger version of 3NF - every functional dependency must have a superkey
Benefits: Reduces redundancy, prevents anomalies (insert, update, delete), saves storage
Denormalization: Intentionally adding redundancy for performance
examples: Before: Student(ID, Name, Course1, Course2, Course3) - violates 1NF
After 1NF: Student(ID, Name), Enrollment(StudentID, Course) - atomic values
After 2NF: Order(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity), Product(ProductID, ProductName)

subject: DBMS
explanation: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for managing and manipulating relational databases. It allows CRUD operations: Create, Read, Update, Delete.
key_points: DDL (Data Definition Language): CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
DML (Data Manipulation Language): SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
DCL (Data Control Language): GRANT, REVOKE
TCL (Transaction Control Language): COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, JOIN are fundamental
Joins: INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, FULL OUTER JOIN
examples: SELECT * FROM Students WHERE Age > 18;
INSERT INTO Students (ID, Name, Age) VALUES (1, 'Alice', 20);
SELECT s.Name FROM Students s INNER JOIN Enrollments e ON s.ID = e.StudentID;

subject: DBMS
explanation: A transaction is a sequence of database operations treated as a single logical unit of work. Transactions must satisfy ACID properties to ensure data integrity.
key_points: Atomicity: All operations succeed or all fail (all-or-nothing)
Consistency: Database moves from one consistent state to another
Isolation: Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other
Durability: Committed transactions are permanently saved even after system failure
COMMIT saves changes; ROLLBACK undoes changes
Concurrency problems: Dirty Read, Non-repeatable Read, Phantom Read
examples: Bank transfer: Deduct from Account A AND Add to Account B - both must happen or neither
If power fails during a transfer, ACID ensures the database is not inconsistent
BEGIN TRANSACTION; UPDATE Accounts SET Balance=Balance-100 WHERE ID=1; COMMIT;

subject: C++
explanation: In C++, a class is a user-defined blueprint that defines attributes (data members) and behaviors (member functions). An object is an instance of a class.
key_points: Class: blueprint/template; Object: instance of a class
Data members: variables that store the object state
Member functions: functions that define object behavior
Access specifiers: public, private, protected
Objects are created using the class name
Dot operator (.) is used to access members of an object
examples: class Car { public: string brand; void drive() { cout << brand << ' is driving'; } };
Car myCar; myCar.brand = 'Toyota'; myCar.drive();
A Student class with attributes name, rollNo and methods study(), takeExam()

subject: C++
explanation: A constructor is a special member function automatically called when an object is created. It has the same name as the class and no return type. Its purpose is to initialize the object data members.
key_points: Same name as the class, no return type
Automatically called when an object is created
Default constructor: no parameters
Parameterized constructor: accepts parameters to initialize members
Copy constructor: creates a new object as a copy of an existing object
Constructor overloading: multiple constructors with different parameter lists
examples: class Student { public: string name; int age; Student(string n, int a) { name=n; age=a; } };
Student s1('Alice', 20); // parameterized constructor called automatically
Student s2 = s1; // copy constructor called

subject: C++
explanation: Inheritance is an OOP concept where a derived class acquires properties and behaviors of a base class. It promotes code reuse and establishes an IS-A relationship.
key_points: Promotes code reuse - derived class inherits base class members
IS-A relationship: Dog IS-A Animal, Car IS-A Vehicle
Types: Single, Multiple, Multilevel, Hierarchical, Hybrid
Derived class can override base class methods
Constructor of base class is called first, then derived class constructor
The virtual keyword enables runtime polymorphism
examples: class Animal { public: void eat() { cout << 'eating'; } };
class Dog : public Animal { public: void bark() { cout << 'woof'; } };
Dog d; d.eat(); d.bark(); // Dog inherits eat() from Animal

subject: C++
explanation: Polymorphism means many forms. In C++, it allows a single interface to represent different underlying forms. Types: compile-time (function overloading) and runtime (virtual functions).
key_points: Compile-time (Static) Polymorphism: Function overloading, Operator overloading
Runtime (Dynamic) Polymorphism: Function overriding using virtual functions
Virtual functions: declared with virtual keyword in base class
Pure virtual functions (=0): make a class abstract
Virtual table (vtable) implements runtime polymorphism
examples: Function overloading: int add(int a, int b); float add(float a, float b);
virtual void sound() in Animal class; Dog overrides to Woof; Cat overrides to Meow
Animal* ptr = new Dog(); ptr->sound(); // prints Woof - runtime polymorphism

subject: C++
explanation: Function overloading allows multiple functions to have the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler selects the correct function based on arguments at compile time.
key_points: Same function name, different parameter lists
Resolved at compile time (static/early binding)
Parameters must differ in: number, type, or order
Return type alone cannot differentiate overloaded functions
Improves code readability
examples: int add(int a, int b); // two integers
float add(float a, float b); // two floats
int add(int a, int b, int c); // three integers
All named add - compiler picks the right one based on arguments

subject: Java
explanation: In Java, a class is a blueprint for creating objects. It defines the data (fields) and behavior (methods). Java is fully object-oriented.
key_points: Class: template/blueprint; Object: instance of a class
Fields (instance variables) store the state of an object
Methods define the behavior of an object
Access modifiers: public, private, protected, default
Objects are created using the new keyword
Java garbage collector automatically frees unused object memory
The this keyword refers to the current object
examples: class Dog { String name; void bark() { System.out.println('Woof!'); } }
Dog myDog = new Dog(); // creating an object
myDog.name = 'Buddy'; myDog.bark(); // accessing members

subject: Java
explanation: Inheritance in Java allows a subclass to inherit fields and methods of a superclass. Java supports single inheritance for classes and multiple inheritance through interfaces using the extends keyword.
key_points: Uses extends keyword for class inheritance
Java supports only single inheritance for classes
Multiple inheritance achieved through interfaces
super keyword refers to the parent class
Method overriding: subclass provides specific implementation of a parent method
@Override annotation confirms you are overriding a parent method
All Java classes implicitly extend Object class
examples: class Animal { void makeSound() { System.out.println('Some sound'); } }
class Cat extends Animal { @Override void makeSound() { System.out.println('Meow'); } }
Cat c = new Cat(); c.makeSound(); // prints Meow

subject: Java
explanation: Exception handling in Java is a mechanism to handle runtime errors gracefully, maintaining normal program flow. Java uses try-catch-finally blocks and throw/throws keywords.
key_points: Exception: an event that disrupts normal program flow
try: block of code that might throw an exception
catch: block that handles the specific exception
finally: block that always executes (cleanup code)
throw: manually throw an exception
throws: declares that a method might throw certain exceptions
Checked exceptions must handle: IOException, SQLException
Unchecked exceptions (runtime): NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
examples: try { int result = 10/0; } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println('Cannot divide by zero'); } finally { System.out.println('Always runs'); }
Custom exception: class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception { ... }

subject: Java
explanation: An interface in Java defines a contract - a set of methods that a class must implement. Interfaces achieve abstraction and multiple inheritance. All methods are public and abstract by default.
key_points: Defines a contract using interface keyword
Uses implements keyword to use an interface
All methods are public and abstract by default (before Java 8)
Java 8+: interfaces can have default and static methods
A class can implement multiple interfaces
Interface variables are public, static, and final by default
examples: interface Drawable { void draw(); }
class Circle implements Drawable { public void draw() { System.out.println('Drawing circle'); } }
class Bird implements Drawable, Flyable { ... } // multiple interfaces

subject: Java
explanation: The Java Collections Framework provides classes and interfaces for storing and manipulating groups of objects. It includes ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap, HashSet, etc.
key_points: List: ordered collection, allows duplicates (ArrayList, LinkedList)
Set: unordered collection, no duplicates (HashSet, TreeSet)
Map: key-value pairs, no duplicate keys (HashMap, TreeMap)
Queue: FIFO structure (LinkedList, PriorityQueue)
Collections class provides utility methods: sort(), reverse(), shuffle()
Generics ensure type safety: ArrayList<String>, HashMap<Integer, String>
examples: ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); list.add('Apple'); list.get(0);
HashMap<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>(); map.put('Alice', 90); map.get('Alice');
HashSet<Integer> set = new HashSet<>(); set.add(1); set.add(1); // size is 1

subject: Computer Networks
explanation: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model is a conceptual framework that standardizes network communication into 7 layers, each with specific responsibilities.
key_points: Layer 7 - Application: User interface (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS)
Layer 6 - Presentation: Data format, encryption, compression
Layer 5 - Session: Manages sessions between applications
Layer 4 - Transport: End-to-end communication (TCP, UDP)
Layer 3 - Network: Logical addressing, routing (IP, ICMP)
Layer 2 - Data Link: Physical addressing MAC, framing (Ethernet, Wi-Fi)
Layer 1 - Physical: Bits over physical medium (cables, signals)
examples: When you send an email, it goes through all 7 layers on sender and receiver
HTTP operates at Application layer; TCP at Transport; IP at Network

subject: Computer Networks
explanation: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable. UDP is connectionless and faster but unreliable. Both are transport layer protocols.
key_points: TCP: Connection-oriented (three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)
TCP: Reliable - guarantees delivery, ordering, and error checking
TCP: Slower due to overhead of acknowledgments
TCP uses: HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, email (SMTP)
UDP: Connectionless - no handshake
UDP: Unreliable but faster - no guarantee of delivery
UDP uses: Video streaming, gaming, VoIP, DNS
examples: Downloading a file uses TCP - every bit must arrive correctly
Video call uses UDP - better to drop a frame than pause the call
DNS uses UDP for quick lookups

subject: Computer Networks
explanation: An IP address is a unique numerical label assigned to each device on a network. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses. Subnetting divides a network into smaller sub-networks.
key_points: IPv4: 32-bit address written as 4 octets (e.g., 192.168.1.100)
IPv6: 128-bit address to solve IPv4 exhaustion
Subnet mask determines network vs host portion
CIDR notation: 192.168.1.0/24 means 24 bits are network bits
NAT maps private IPs to public IP
examples: 192.168.1.0/24: network with 256 addresses, 254 usable hosts
10.0.0.1 is a private IP (home router default gateway)
DNS translates domain names to IP addresses

subject: Computer Networks
explanation: HTTP is the protocol for transmitting web pages. HTTPS is the encrypted version using SSL/TLS. HTTP operates on port 80, HTTPS on port 443.
key_points: HTTP: stateless, application-layer protocol for web communication
Methods: GET (retrieve), POST (submit), PUT (update), DELETE (remove)
Status codes: 200 OK, 301 Redirect, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error
HTTPS = HTTP + SSL/TLS encryption for security
HTTPS prevents eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks
examples: GET /index.html HTTP/1.1 - retrieving a web page
POST /login with username and password in request body
200 OK means success; 404 Not Found means page does not exist

subject: Data Structures
explanation: An array stores elements of the same data type in contiguous memory locations. Elements are accessed using an index starting from 0. Arrays have a fixed size.
key_points: Fixed size, contiguous memory allocation
Zero-indexed: first element at index 0, last at index n-1
Access time: O(1) - direct access by index
Insertion/Deletion: O(n) - elements must be shifted
Search: O(n) linear, O(log n) if sorted (binary search)
Static arrays vs Dynamic arrays (ArrayList in Java, vector in C++)
examples: Matrix: int matrix[3][3] for a 3x3 grid
Storing marks of 100 students: int marks[100];

subject: Data Structures
explanation: A linked list stores elements in non-contiguous memory locations. Each node contains data and a pointer to the next node. Unlike arrays, linked lists can grow and shrink dynamically.
key_points: Each node has: data + pointer to next node
Head pointer points to the first node; null pointer at the end
Dynamic size - can grow/shrink at runtime
Insertion/Deletion: O(1) if position known, O(n) to find position
Access: O(n) - must traverse from head
Types: Singly, Doubly, Circular linked list
examples: 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40 -> NULL (singly linked list)
NULL <- 10 <-> 20 <-> 30 -> NULL (doubly linked list)
Browser history: each page links to previous and next page

subject: Data Structures
explanation: A stack is a linear data structure following LIFO (Last In, First Out). The last element added is the first one removed, like a stack of plates.
key_points: LIFO: Last In, First Out
Push: add element to top
Pop: remove element from top
Peek/Top: view top element without removing
All operations: O(1) time complexity
Applications: Function call stack, undo operations, expression evaluation, backtracking
examples: Browser back button: pages are pushed as you navigate, popped when you go back
Undo (Ctrl+Z) in text editors uses a stack
Checking balanced parentheses: push '(' and pop when ')' is encountered

subject: Data Structures
explanation: A queue is a linear data structure following FIFO (First In, First Out). The first element added is the first one removed, like a real-world queue at a bank.
key_points: FIFO: First In, First Out
Enqueue: add element to the rear
Dequeue: remove element from the front
Types: Simple Queue, Circular Queue, Priority Queue, Deque
Applications: CPU scheduling, print spooling, BFS traversal
Enqueue/Dequeue: O(1) time complexity
examples: Printer queue: first document sent is first document printed
Bank customer line: first customer to arrive is first served
BFS (Breadth First Search) uses a queue

subject: Data Structures
explanation: A BST is a binary tree where for each node, all left subtree values are smaller, and all right subtree values are larger. This enables efficient searching, insertion, and deletion.
key_points: For each node: left subtree values < node value < right subtree values
Search, Insert, Delete: O(log n) average, O(n) worst case (unbalanced)
In-order traversal gives elements in sorted order
Balanced BST (AVL tree, Red-Black tree): guarantees O(log n)
Applications: Dictionaries, database indexing, priority queues
examples: BST with root 50: left subtree has 30, 20, 40; right subtree has 70, 60, 80
Searching 40: start at 50 (go left), check 30 (go right), find 40

subject: Data Structures
explanation: Sorting algorithms arrange elements in a specific order. Common algorithms: Bubble Sort, Merge Sort, Quick Sort each with different time and space complexities.
key_points: Bubble Sort: O(n squared) - repeatedly swap adjacent elements if out of order
Selection Sort: O(n squared) - find minimum, place at beginning
Insertion Sort: O(n squared) - good for nearly sorted data
Merge Sort: O(n log n) - divide and conquer; stable; uses extra space O(n)
Quick Sort: O(n log n) average, O(n squared) worst - partition around pivot
Stable sort preserves relative order of equal elements
examples: Merge Sort divides array into halves, sorts each, then merges
Quick Sort picks a pivot and partitions smaller elements left, larger right
Insertion Sort: like sorting playing cards in hand
